doc.title: Howard Levy interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, November 11, 2025

title: Why diatonic harmonica rather than chromatic
summary: Levy explains he loved blues harmonica sound and chose to push the diatonic instrument, though he also learned chromatic.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: What the blues is, and why every jazz player needs it

blocks.x: Why did you not go in that direction with the chromatic harmonica?

Well the reason why I started playing the harmonica was that my buddies and I in high school and we started with the rock bands and then we started playing blues, and I fell in love with the sound of the blues harmonica and all the Chicago guys, you know Paul Butterfield, James Cotton, Little Walter – that sound. And you can’t get that sound on the chromatic. So you know once I discovered how to play chromatically on the diatonic harmonica I thought well why can’t I take this instrument into the same places that, you know, sax players, trumpet players, I mean like pianists. You know I want to take this instrument as far as I can rather than say I’m going to give up here when the music gets to a certain point I’m going to stop this and play this. Because this instrument doesn’t do the same thing that this instrument does. And this instrument doesn’t exactly do what this one does either. So it was a choice. Because I know how to play the chromatic. I taught

myself how to play it in the early and mid-1970s when I was trying to get better at reading music on harmonica. Because I found it too difficult to read on this instrument while I was doing all of these manipulations with the inside of my mouth and all this stuff to get all the pitches. And gradually I became a very good reader on this. But yeah, this, the bluesy, soulfulness of this instrument, which is a total accident of design, is what appeals to me.
